items.title: While You Were Sleeping: 5 stories you might have missed, Nov 21, 2026 | The Straits Times
items.excerpt: ## Trump, Xi agree military AI decisions should involve humans US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed humans should always be involved in military decisions that use artificial intelligence technologies, even as the two countries compete for AI supremacy, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Nov 20. Bessent told CNBC after returning from Trump’s meeting with Xi in Shenzhen, China, that the agreement was among the major achievements of Trump’s trip to Asia. “I think it was very important that President Trump and President Xi agreed that humans should always be involved in any military decisions that SI makes, and the SI should not be allowed to be autonomous for major military actions,” Bessent said - referring to the Trump administration’s preferred term for the technology, “super intelligence.” Bessent said that the US-China agreement on military use of the technology, requiring human involvement and other safeguards, would not be affected by the two countries’ competition for AI supremacy. He added that US AI labs needed to maintain their technological lead as the best defence against “dangerous” Chinese AI models that are being used in cyberattacks. ## Trump says he, Putin had ‘very good’ talks on Ukraine US President Donald Trump said on Nov 20 that he and Russian leader Vladimir Putin held “very good” talks on Ukraine during their meeting in China, but said he didn’t want to discuss security guarantees for Ukraine without a deal. “We’re having very good talks. I think there’s a real good chance that we can get it done,” Trump said at a White House news conference after his trip to Asia, where he met with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Trump spoke to Putin, whom he called a friend, separately during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting in Shenzhen, China, this week. ## Wall St ends sharply lower on AI selloff ... US stocks extended their rout on Nov 20, and the S&P 500 and the Dow both confirmed corrections after Anthropic’s momentous debut fell flat, exacerbating worries about the AI trade that has driven this year’s stock market rally. All three major US equity indexes ended sharply lower. The Dow and the S&P 500 are now more than 10% below their record closing highs, confirming both indexes have entered a correction.

items.title: Fed’s Cook says rate hikes needed to lower high inflation By Reuters
items.excerpt: Nov 20 (Reuters) - Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook on Friday made a case for more interest rate hikes, saying the US central bank’s current policy rate is not high enough to deal with inflation levels she views with "great concern." "In a different environment, the (Federal Open Market) Committee could afford to be patient, but I continue to believe that in this economic climate we do not have that luxury," given how high inflation is and for how long it has been above the Fed’s 2% target, Cook said in the text of a speech to be presented at a central bank conference in Chile. Cook said the quarter-percentage-point rate hike the Fed delivered at its September 15-16 policy meeting was not enough to moderate current levels of inflation. What’s more, "inflation data received since the September rate increase, including reports last week, fail to provide me with sufficient evidence that inflation is returning to a sustainable path," she said. "There is little evidence inflation is declining."

items.title: Fed's Cook says inflation has been above target for 67 months and defends her call for a second rise | FinanceInTime
items.excerpt: Published Nov 21, 2026, 01:11 UTC 3 min read ... Federal Reserve Governor Lisa D. Cook said on Friday that inflation has exceeded the Fed's 2% target for 67 months and that she wanted a second rate increase in October, according to the text of her speech at a Central Bank of Chile conference in Santiago. ## A dissent explained in two reasons Cook spoke at the 29th annual conference of the Central Bank of Chile. She said the views were her own and not necessarily those of her colleagues on the Fed Board or the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC). The FOMC raised the target range for the federal funds rate in September to 3.75%-4%, Cook said. At its October meeting, the committee voted to hold the rate steady. She dissented and preferred a further quarter-point increase. She gave two reasons. The first was that financial conditions are "too accommodative" while inflation is above target. Cook said the current stance of policy "does not appear to be curtailing the AI buildout" and that equity prices continue to support consumer spending. The second was urgency: waiting longer, she said, "risks getting behind the curve," and if that happens, "additional and larger rate increases may be required later to catch up." Cook said she is skeptical that September's single quarter-point increase will be enough to change the path of inflation. She added that the number and size of future adjustments should be informed by how the economy reacts to the Fed's actions. ## Inflation at 3.8% and a broad list of prices Based on data released the previous week, Cook said, the 12-month change in the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index was estimated at 3.8% in October. Core PCE, which excludes food and energy, was 3.2%. She said the most recent release showed prices rising briskly in a very broad range of categories, including airfare, appliances, furniture, hotels and restaurants. That point matters to her argument that energy is not the only source of pressure: the core measure, she said, "underscores that, while energy is a significant contributor to inflation, the sources of price pressure facing American families are increasingly varied." ## Growth and jobs give her little reason to wait Cook described an economy that is accelerating. GDP rose at a 3.4% annual pace in the third quarter, and real household spending rose at an annualized 3.8%. The unemployment rate was 4.1% in October, and payrolls climbed by 165,000. She tied part of the acceleration to the AI infrastructure buildout. Companies have announced plans for more than $2 trillion in specific data center construction projects in the US, Cook said, and only a fraction of that has been realized so far.

items.title: AI is fueling "disturbingly high" inflation, Chicago Fed president says - CBS News
items.excerpt: The boom in AI data center construction is adding to the nation's "borderline disturbingly high" inflation, with the sector's massive business investment indirectly contributing to rising service prices, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago President Austan Goolsbee told reporters on Thursday. "The AI boom is contributing to the potential of overheating in the economy," Goolsbee said. "I find it hard to look at it any other way when you are getting major business investment, almost an unprecedented level of business investment." Goolsbee, who will become a voting member of the interest rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee in January, declined to forecast the central bank's next moves on interest rates. But he said the Fed's decisions will be determined by whether U.S. inflation is on track to return to the central bank's annual 2% target.

items.title: Democrat-controlled Congress faces task of reforming Trump’s immigration agenda | U.S. | EL PAÍS English
items.excerpt: Washington - Nov 21, 2026 - 05:00 CET After the economy, the aggressive immigration policy implemented by the administration of Donald Trump was the main reason U.S. voters punished the Republican Party and gave the Democrats a historic victory in the midterms. The Democratic Party will hold a majority in the United States Congress starting January 3. In the House of Representatives it will occupy at least 256 of the 435 seats after taking 42 seats from the Republicans. In the Senate it will hold 55 seats, eight more than before. The victors face the arduous task of changing an immigration system widely regarded as broken and that Congress has been unable to reform for decades. Amid Democratic euphoria over the win, ending Trump’s anti-immigrant crusade has emerged as one of their legislative priorities. Whether they succeed will not depend solely on them. A Democrat-controlled Congress will coincide with the last two years of Trump’s term. The president, as is typical for him, has sent mixed signals about how he wants to address immigration. Just a week ago he admitted in an interview on CBS’s 60 Minutes that his immigration policy had been too harsh and that people who were taxpaying workers had been deported. Hours after the interview was recorded, however, he promoted the architect of the administration’s most hardline immigration stance, Stephen Miller, to White House chief of staff. In later remarks, Trump clarified that there would be no amnesty and that his policy had not changed. “We’ve seen this time and again. Trump says something moderately reasonable on immigration and then Stephen Miller gives him a dressing-down, after which he comes out with a new commitment to maximalist positions,” says Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, senior researcher at the American Immigration Council and one of the immigration experts who has testified in Congress about the administration’s abuses in this area. But the reality is that the landscape has changed with the Democrats taking control of Congress. Markwayne Mullin, secretary of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), said Trump encouraged him to work with the Democrats on immigration reform after telling him he had received many calls about the issue. Democratic lawmakers have confirmed the same. “We’ve had some conversations and, without going into details, I think there are common ground points that will allow us to reach an agreement,” said Representative Henry Cuéllar of Texas at a pro-immigration reform event held last week in front of the Capitol. ... Among the immigration bills that have so far failed in the House of Representatives, one stands a better chance of succeeding: the Dream Act, a bill that grants legal residency and opens a path to citizenship for foreigners who arrived undocumented as children. Many are beneficiaries of the DACA program (Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals) and have grown up, studied, worked and formed families in the only country they consider home. Trump has tried to end the program, created under the Barack Obama administration, during his two terms, but courts have blocked him. The so-called “dreamers” are the migrants with the broadest support across the political spectrum. The bill needs only one more Republican representative’s signature to be brought to the floor of the House. “My American Dream and Promise discharge petition has 217 signatures. 214 Democrats and three Republicans. We just need one more Republican signature to get it to the finish line and force a vote. We cannot wait any longer,” Representative Sylvia García, co-author of the Dream Act, wrote on social media after attending the same event in front of Congress on November 11. ... In addition to the Dream Act, there is another legislative proposal with broad bipartisan support: the Dignity Act, which provides for the legalization of undocumented migrants who have lived in the country for years, while also strengthening border security and reforming visa programs. ... Even if the bills pass both chambers, uncertainty remains over whether Trump — who has the power to veto them — will sign them.
